content: The coronary anatomy is divided into specific segments to identify the location of the culprit artery. These segments are defined as follows: 1. No Lesion (0): No angiographic evidence of a lesion greater than 50% is present. 2. Proximal Right Coronary Artery (R1): This segment extends from the origin (ostium) of the right coronary artery to the first of the three longest acute marginal branches. 3. Mid Right Coronary Artery (R2): This segment begins at the origin of the first acute marginal branch and extends to the origin of the third acute marginal branch. 4. Distal Right Coronary Artery (R3): This segment starts at the origin of the third acute marginal branch and extends to the origin of the posterior descending artery. 5. Right Posterolateral Artery (R4): Also known as the right retroventricular artery, this is the continuation of the right coronary artery beyond the posterior descending artery. It supplies blood to the right posterior and inferior arteries in large right-dominant systems, to the right inferior branch in small right-dominant systems, and is absent in left or balanced dominant systems. 6. Acute Marginal Arteries (A1, A2, A3): These are the three longest branches arising from the right coronary artery, supplying the right ventricular wall. They are numbered from proximal to distal. 7. Right Posterior Descending Artery (RD): Also called the right posterior interventricular artery, this vessel runs in the posterior interventricular groove in all systems except left-dominant ones. It supplies septal perforator branches and is one of the three longest branches on the inferior wall of the heart when present. 8. Right Inferior Artery (RI): This artery arises from the fourth segment of the right coronary artery and supplies the inferior wall. In small right-dominant systems, it is the most distal branch of the right coronary artery, while in large right-dominant systems, it arises proximal to the posterior descending artery. It is one of the three longest branches on the inferior wall when present. 9. Right Posterior Artery (RP): This is the most distal branch of the right coronary artery, present only in large right-dominant systems. It is one of the three longest branches on the inferior wall when present. 10. Left Main Coronary Artery (LM): This segment extends from the origin of the left coronary artery to its bifurcation into the left anterior descending (LAD) and circumflex (LCx) arteries. 11. Proximal Left Anterior Descending Artery (L1): This segment extends from the bifurcation of the left main coronary artery to the origin of the first septal branch. 12. Mid Left Anterior Descending Artery (L2): This segment begins at the origin of the first septal branch and extends to the origin of the third septal branch. 13. Distal Left Anterior Descending Artery (L3): This segment starts at the origin of the third septal branch and extends to the apex of the left ventricle. If no third septal branch is present, the segment begins halfway between the first septal branch and the apex. 14. Left Anterior Descending Artery Terminus (L4): This is the continuation of the LAD beyond the apex of the left ventricle in cases where the LAD is a wrap-around variant. 15. First Diagonal Artery (D1): This is the first of the three longest branches off the LAD, supplying the anterolateral wall of the left ventricle. 16. Second Diagonal Artery (D2): This is the second of the three longest branches off the LAD, also supplying the anterolateral wall of the left ventricle. 17. Third Diagonal Artery (D3): This is the third of the three longest branches off the LAD, supplying the anterolateral wall of the left ventricle. It often arises where the LAD angles toward the apex in a right anterior oblique (RAO) projection. 18. Septal Arteries (S1, S2, S3): These are the three largest branches off the LAD that supply the interventricular septum. 19. Median Ramus (MR): Also called the intermedius ramus, this artery originates between the LAD and LCx. When present, the left main artery trifurcates, and the median ramus is the middle branch. It is grouped with the LCx unless otherwise specified by trial protocols. 20. Proximal Circumflex Artery (C1): This segment extends from the origin of the LCx to the origin of the first marginal or obtuse marginal branch. 21. Mid Circumflex Artery (C2): This segment begins at the origin of the first marginal or obtuse marginal branch and extends to the origin of the second marginal or obtuse marginal branch. 22. Distal Circumflex Artery (C3): This segment extends from the origin of the second marginal or obtuse marginal branch to the termination of the LCx in large right-dominant systems or to the origin of the circumflex posterior branch in other dominance patterns. 23. Left Posterolateral Artery (C4): In left-dominant or balanced systems, this is the distal continuation of the LCx in the atrioventricular groove. It supplies the left posterior descending artery and circumflex inferior artery in left-dominant systems or just the circumflex inferior artery in balanced systems. 24. Circumflex Posterior Artery (CP): This branch originates at the distal end of the third segment of the LCx and supplies the inferior wall of the heart. It is one of the three longest branches on the inferior wall when present. 25. Circumflex Inferior Artery (CI): This artery arises from the junction between the third and fourth segments of the LCx and supplies the inferior wall. In balanced systems, it is the most distal branch of the LCx, while in left-dominant systems, it arises proximal to the left posterior descending artery. 26. Left Posterior Descending Artery (CD): In left-dominant systems, this is the distal continuation of the LCx, traveling in the interventricular groove and supplying septal perforators at the base of the heart. It is one of the three longest branches on the inferior wall when present. 27. Marginal Arteries (M1, M2, M3): These are the three longest branches off the LCx that supply the lateral wall of the left ventricle. If a large dominating artery is present, it is referred to as an obtuse marginal artery. 28. Obtuse Marginal Arteries (OM1, OM2, OM3): These are large branching arteries that dominate the lateral left ventricular wall. They consist of anterior and posterior branches that share a common trunk. Only one obtuse marginal artery is present, and it is numbered based on its origin relative to the marginal arteries. 29. Obtuse Marginal Trunk (OT): This is the common trunk connecting the anterior and posterior branches of an obtuse marginal artery to the LCx. 30. Anterior Branch of the Obtuse Marginal Artery (OA): This is the anterior branch of a large obtuse marginal artery. 31. Posterior Branch of the Obtuse Marginal Artery (OP): This is the posterior branch of a large obtuse marginal artery. 32. Saphenous Vein Grafts (SVG): These include grafts to the LAD (SVGLAD), LCx (SVGCX), right coronary artery (SVGRCA), posterior descending artery (SVGPDA), obtuse marginal artery (SVGOM), and diagonal artery (SVGD). 33. Internal Mammary Artery Grafts: These include the left internal mammary artery to the LAD (LIMA) and the right internal mammary artery to the LAD (RIMA). Additional Definitions: If a lesion occurs at a branch point, it is considered part of the proximal vessel adjacent to the branch point. If a lesion involves both the parent vessel and a side branch at a branch point (e.g., a trifurcation lesion involving the LAD and a diagonal branch), the larger parent vessel is defined as the culprit.
